newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lagardere defends corner on Thomson-CSF.
newsitem.headline: Lagardere defends corner on Thomson-CSF.

text.p: Missiles conglomerate Lagardere hit back on Monday at weekend reports its rival Alcatel Alsthom would win a key role in Thomson-CSF after plans to privatise the French company were called off.

Lagardere and Alcatel both bid for the defence electronics giant in the latest privatisation which was cancelled by the new Socialist-led government on Friday and in last year's botched selloff of state parent firm Thomson SA.
Lagardere unexpectedly won the previous centre-right government's backing for the first attempted sale but it had to be abandoned after criticism from the privatisation commission.
"Governments change but the same rumours are being repeated and still favour the same group, Alcatel," a Lagardere spokesman said, reading from a prepared statement.
"Therefore, as happened last year, it is being said that they have won in advance before even the new process has begun."
He declined fuurther comment on the government decision.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's office announced on Friday it was cancelling the sale of a 58 percent state shareholding in Thomson-CSF. The month-old government said it would draw up a new plan within weeks involving Thomson-CSF as a pole of the French defence industry with a "decisive" public stake.

French newspapers widely reported at the weekend that while holding onto the state's current investment, the government was willing to see its percentage in Thomson-CSF fall indirectly below halfway to reach a blocking minority near 40 percent.
That would allow extra capital to be found from private investors in an enlarged organisation or a new joint entity.
Newspapers said the new capital structure would be drawn from four main sources -- the government, state aerospace firm Aerospatiale, Alcatel Alsthom and Dassault.

Warplane manufacturer Dassault has teamed up with Alcatel in the Thomson discussions, providing what commentators said would be an attractive French solution for Jospin. He has pledged to put national interest first in weighing selloffs.

But German's Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa), which had partnered Lagardere, warned on Monday that wider restucturing of the European aerospace industry would continue despite the cancellation of the Thomson-CSF sale.

The cancellation is a potential source of friction between Jospin's left-wing team and conservative President Jacques Chirac, who has been handed his second rebuff on Thomson since he launched the original selloff idea in February last year.
Chirac was expected to be quizzed on Jospin's decision during a key Bastille Day television interview later on Monday.
